subject: combined-science

items.q: Which statement describes the electricity supply in a UK home?
items.correct: An alternating supply, of about 230 V, with a frequency of 50 Hz
items.misconception: A direct supply, of about 230 V, with a frequency of 50 Hz
items.why: Students meet dc first with cells, and see that a mains appliance runs smoothly with no visible flickering. A steady effect is read as a steady, one-directional potential difference. A steady effect does not mean a steady direction. The mains potential difference completes 50 full cycles every second; appliances are simply too slow to respond to each reversal.
items.random_wrong: An alternating supply, of 50 V, at a frequency of 230 Hz

items.q: What is the difference between a direct and an alternating potential difference?
items.correct: A direct pd acts one way only; an alternating pd keeps reversing
items.misconception: A direct pd stays the same size, but an alternating pd changes size
items.why: The word 'alternating' is read as 'changing', and a graph that rises and falls is described only by its height. Students who ignore the zero line never notice the change of sign. Look at the zero line on the trace. An alternating potential difference goes below zero as well as above it, and below zero means the push is the other way round the circuit.
items.random_wrong: A direct pd is always low, but an alternating pd is always big

items.q: A student connects an oscilloscope first to a cell and then to a low-voltage supply at mains frequency. Which description of the two traces is correct?
items.correct: The cell gives a flat line; the mains trace crosses zero
items.misconception: Both traces are flat lines, but the mains line sits much higher up
items.why: Students meet dc first with cells, and see that a mains appliance runs smoothly with no visible flickering. A steady effect is read as a steady, one-directional potential difference. A steady effect does not mean a steady direction. The mains potential difference completes 50 full cycles every second; appliances are simply too slow to respond to each reversal.
items.random_wrong: The cell trace crosses the zero line; the mains gives a flat line

items.q: The UK mains supply has a frequency of 50 Hz. What does this tell you?
items.correct: The pd goes through 50 cycles each second
items.misconception: The pd completes 50 full cycles every minute
items.why: Two numbers are memorised as a pair and then reattached to the wrong quantity, and 'per second' is confused with 'per minute' by analogy with heart rate or engine revs. Hertz means cycles per second, so 50 Hz is 50 complete cycles every second. The potential difference is the 230 V figure.
items.random_wrong: The supply frequency is actually 230 Hz

items.q: Most electrical appliances are connected to the mains using three-core cable. What are the three cores?
items.correct: The live wire, the neutral wire and the earth wire
items.misconception: Two live wires together with one neutral wire
items.why: The fuse is the other part of a plug that students remember, and 'three cores' is recalled as a number before the roles of the wires are learnt. The three cores are live, neutral and earth. The fuse is a component in the plug, fitted in the live wire; it is not one of the cores.
items.random_wrong: The live wire, the neutral wire and a fuse wire

items.q: The insulation on the wires in a three-core cable is colour coded. Which row gives the colours correctly?
items.correct: Live brown, neutral blue, earth green and yellow
items.misconception: Live brown, neutral blue, earth is plain green
items.why: Green alone is the colour students associate with the ground and with 'safe', and the striping is a detail that is easily dropped when recalling. The earth wire is specified as green and yellow stripes. The two-colour stripe is deliberately unlike any other wire, so it cannot be mistaken.
items.random_wrong: Live blue, neutral brown, earth plain green

items.q: A wire inside a plug is covered in blue insulation. What is the job of this wire?
items.correct: It completes the circuit back to the supply
items.misconception: It carries the alternating pd from the supply
items.why: Both colours are dark and neither has an obvious link to its wire, so the pair is remembered as 'brown and blue' without which is which. Older red-and-black house wiring adds to the confusion. Use a fixed link: bRown for the Risky wire (live), Blue for the wire that goes Back to the supply (neutral). Live brown, neutral blue.
items.random_wrong: It carries current away only if there is a fault

items.q: Why is the insulation covering each wire in a cable colour coded?
items.correct: So that each wire can be identified easily
items.misconception: So that each wire can carry a different sized current
items.why: Colour coding is met elsewhere as a scale (resistor bands, hot and cold taps, hazard labels), so students expect the colour to encode a quantity. The colours are labels, not measurements. The insulation covering each wire is colour coded only for easy identification.
items.random_wrong: Because coloured plastics insulate at a higher voltage

items.q: What is the job of the live wire in a mains circuit?
items.correct: It carries the alternating potential difference from the supply
items.misconception: It takes the current back to the supply after the appliance
items.why: Both colours are dark and neither has an obvious link to its wire, so the pair is remembered as 'brown and blue' without which is which. Older red-and-black house wiring adds to the confusion. Use a fixed link: bRown for the Risky wire (live), Blue for the wire that goes Back to the supply (neutral). Live brown, neutral blue.
items.random_wrong: It carries a current only if a fault develops in the case

items.q: What is the purpose of the earth wire in an appliance with a metal case?
items.correct: It is a safety wire that stops the appliance becoming live
items.misconception: It completes the circuit so that a current can pass round
items.why: Students know a circuit needs a return path and know the earth wire goes to the ground, so they merge the two ideas into one wire. The neutral wire is the return path that completes the circuit. The earth wire is a safety wire, there to stop the appliance becoming live.
items.random_wrong: It carries the used current away to the ground all the time

items.q: A kettle is plugged in and working. Which row gives the potential differences correctly?
items.correct: Live to earth about 230 V; neutral to earth about 0 V
items.misconception: Live to earth about 230 V; neutral to earth about 230 V
items.why: Both wires carry the same current, so students assume they must be at the same potential, or they split the supply pd evenly between the pair. Potential difference is measured between two points. Live sits about 230 V above earth; neutral sits at, or close to, 0 V, which is why it is the live wire that is dangerous.
items.random_wrong: Live to earth about 115 V; neutral to earth also 115 V

items.q: When does a current pass along the earth wire of an appliance?
items.correct: Only when there is a fault
items.why: Students who think current is used up look for somewhere for it to go, and a wire that runs into the ground is an obvious destination. The working circuit is live in, neutral out. The earth wire is a safety wire: it is at 0 V and no current passes along it unless a fault connects it to the live wire.
items.random_wrong: All the time it is plugged in

items.q: A lamp is switched off at a switch in the mains circuit, but is still plugged in. Why can the live wire still be dangerous?
items.correct: It is still at about 230 V relative to earth up to the open switch
items.misconception: Opening the switch only lowers the pd to a smaller, safer value
items.why: Students learn that an open switch stops the current, and then treat 'no current' as meaning 'nothing there'. Potential difference is quietly assumed to vanish with the current. An open switch only breaks the path. The supply is still connected, so the live wire on the supply side stays at about 230 V relative to earth and can still give a shock.
items.random_wrong: The neutral wire feeds a current back along the live wire

items.q: A person changes a bulb without unplugging the lamp. The switch is open. Standing on a concrete floor, they touch the live contact and receive a shock. Why?
items.correct: The contact is still at 230 V, so a current passes through them
items.misconception: The earth wire pushes a current out of the ground up through them
items.why: Students who think current is used up look for somewhere for it to go, and a wire that runs into the ground is an obvious destination. The working circuit is live in, neutral out. The earth wire is a safety wire: it is at 0 V and no current passes along it unless a fault connects it to the live wire.
items.random_wrong: Their body completes the circuit between live and neutral

items.q: A frayed cable lets the bare live wire touch a metal water pipe that runs into the ground. Why is this dangerous?
items.correct: There is 230 V across the path, so a large current passes
items.misconception: No current can pass at all, so the wire overheats and melts
items.why: The 0 V label is read as 'no electricity here', rather than as one end of a 230 V potential difference. It is the difference that matters. Live at 230 V and earth at 0 V gives about 230 V across the path, and with little resistance the current is large enough to cause burns or fire.
items.random_wrong: The neutral is at 230 V too, so 460 V drives it

items.q: Why is touching the live wire while standing on wet ground so dangerous, even though only one wire is touched?
items.correct: A current passes through them to earth
items.misconception: The ground is always carrying current, so it shocks them
items.why: Students who think current is used up look for somewhere for it to go, and a wire that runs into the ground is an obvious destination. The working circuit is live in, neutral out. The earth wire is a safety wire: it is at 0 V and no current passes along it unless a fault connects it to the live wire.
items.random_wrong: Only 115 V, half the supply, acts across them

items.q: Which supplies ac, a cell or the mains?
items.correct: The mains supplies ac; a cell or battery supplies a direct potential difference.
items.misconception: The cell gives the alternating supply, because chemicals keep moving inside it, and the mains gives a direct supply.
items.why: The two labels are learnt as a pair of words without being attached to a source, so they are as easily swapped as remembered. A cell has a fixed positive and a fixed negative terminal, so its potential difference cannot reverse: it is dc. Mains electricity is the ac supply.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is touching only the live wire dangerous?
items.correct: Your body provides a connection from the live wire to earth, so a current passes through you.
items.misconception: You are only in danger if you touch the live wire and the neutral wire at the same time, so one hand on one wire is safe.
items.why: Circuit diagrams show a loop between two terminals, so students look for two wires and forget that the ground itself is the second connection. Earth is the other side of the supply. Standing on the ground while touching the live wire completes a path from 230 V to 0 V through your body.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
